(1) we show that the split-state leakage model, in the CRS and no-randomness model, is equivalent to the split-state tampering model, and (2) we construct a non-malleable code with respect to splitstate tampering, in the CRS (and no-randomness) model, which can be used to construct a split-state secure functionality.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: can we algorithmically defend cryptographic devices from split-state attacks?

the following question: Can cryptographic functions be made resilient to continual leakage and tamper attacks, without requiring the hardware to have random access, and without requiring the attacker to be computationally bounded?
the question of whether cryptographic algorithms can be used to secure against physical side channel and tamper attacks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our work provides an algorithmic defense for cryptographic functionality against continual split-state leakage attacks and tampering attacks, and that this is the best possible.
our work provides a simple and modular solution to the problem of protecting against continual split-state leakage, in a model that is realistic for hardware implementations.

our construction provides the first known algorithmic defenses from continual split-state tampering and leakage attacks, and that it is impossible, in the CRS-model, to provide algorithmic defenses from arbitrary continual tampering and leakage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
We give the first general algorithmic defense from continual split-state attacks, which can be used to secure any cryptographic functionality.
we provide an algorithmic solution for the split-state model, which is impossible for the general leakage and tampering model, and our solution is simpler than prior work.

we show that the split-state leakage and split-state tampering models are equivalent in the sense that any functionality can be securely implemented under one model, if and only if it can be implemented under the other.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the split-state model can be a useful abstraction for designing algorithmic defenses against side channel and tamper attacks.
, in the absence of randomness, split-state leakage is the only type of leakage that can be algorithmically protected from.

, for a wide variety of applications, we can now replace the expensive and error-prone task of designing tamper-resistant hardware with an algorithmically simple and efficient task of designing tampered-resistant algorithms.
